title: KVPY — Chemistry | Qualitative Analysis
description: Subject-wise test on Qualitative Analysis (Chemistry) for KVPY. 25Q.
subject: kvpy-chemistry

questions.question: What is the common group reagent for the precipitation of Group I cations (Pb²⁺, Ag⁺, Hg₂²⁺) in qualitative analysis?

options.explanation: H₂S in acidic medium is used for Group II cations.
(NH₄)₂CO₃ in ammoniacal medium is not the common group reagent for Group I cations.
Dilute HCl is the common group reagent for the precipitation of Group I cations.

options.text: NH₄OH in the presence of NH₄Cl
options.explanation: NH₄OH in the presence of NH₄Cl is used for Group III cations.

questions.explanation: Dilute HCl precipitates Group I cations as their chlorides (AgCl, PbCl₂, Hg₂Cl₂), which are insoluble in water. These are then further separated based on their solubility in hot water and ammonia.
questions.subject: kvpy-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following metal hydroxides is amphoteric and will dissolve in both strong acid and strong base?

options.explanation: Fe(OH)₃ is a basic hydroxide and does not dissolve in strong bases.
Cu(OH)₂ is a basic hydroxide and does not dissolve in strong bases.
Ca(OH)₂ is a basic hydroxide and does not dissolve in strong bases.
Al(OH)₃ is an amphoteric hydroxide that dissolves in both strong acid and strong base.

questions.explanation: Amphoteric hydroxides react with both acids and bases. Al(OH)₃ is a white gelatinous precipitate that reacts with acid to form Al³⁺ and with strong base (like NaOH) to form the soluble tetrahydroxoaluminate(III) ion, [Al(OH)₄]⁻.
questions.subject: kvpy-chemistry

questions.question: A colorless solution gives a white precipitate with dilute HCl. This precipitate is completely soluble in hot water. When H₂S gas is passed through the hot filtrate, no precipitate is formed. However, upon adding NH₄Cl and NH₄OH, a white gelatinous precipitate is obtained, which dissolves in excess NaOH. The original solution contains:

options.explanation: Ag⁺ and Zn²⁺ do not match the observed precipitates.
Fe³⁺ does not form a white gelatinous precipitate with NH₄Cl and NH₄OH.
Pb²⁺ and Al³⁺ match the observed precipitates.
Hg₂²⁺ and Mg²⁺ do not match the observed precipitates.

questions.explanation: The white precipitate with dilute HCl indicates the presence of Pb²⁺. The absence of a precipitate with H₂S gas indicates the absence of Group II cations. The white gelatinous precipitate with NH₄Cl and NH₄OH indicates the presence of Al³⁺.
questions.subject: kvpy-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following metal ions imparts a characteristic crimson red color to the Bunsen flame test?

options.explanation: Na⁺ gives a persistent golden yellow flame.
K⁺ gives a lilac (pale violet) flame.
Sr²⁺ gives a characteristic crimson red flame.
Ba²⁺ gives an apple green flame.

questions.explanation: Sr²⁺ gives a characteristic crimson red flame.
questions.subject: kvpy-chemistry

questions.question: A salt gives a deep blue coloration with a solution of FeSO₄ followed by concentrated H₂SO₄. This confirms the presence of which anion?

options.explanation: SO₄²⁻ does not give a deep blue coloration with FeSO₄ and H₂SO₄.
Br⁻ does not give a deep blue coloration with FeSO₄ and H₂SO₄.
NO₃⁻ gives a deep blue coloration with FeSO₄ and H₂SO₄, known as the brown ring test.
Cl⁻ does not give a deep blue coloration with FeSO₄ and H₂SO₄.

questions.explanation: The brown ring test is a characteristic test for nitrate ions (NO₃⁻).
questions.subject: kvpy-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following cations forms a white precipitate with dilute HCl, which is soluble in hot water?

options.explanation: Lead(II) chloride (PbCl₂) is sparingly soluble in cold water but significantly soluble in hot water.
Silver chloride (AgCl) is insoluble in hot water.
Mercury(I) chloride (Hg₂Cl₂) is insoluble in hot water.
Copper(II) ions do not form a white precipitate with dilute HCl.

questions.explanation: This question tests knowledge of Group I cations. Group I cations (Ag⁺, Pb²⁺, Hg₂²⁺) form insoluble chlorides with dilute HCl. Among these, lead(II) chloride (PbCl₂) is sparingly soluble in cold water but significantly soluble in hot water, distinguishing it from AgCl and Hg₂Cl₂, which remain insoluble in hot water.
questions.subject: kvpy-chemistry

questions.question: What is the color of the precipitate formed when H2S gas is passed through an acidic solution containing Cu2+ ions?

options.explanation: The precipitate is not white.
The precipitate is not yellow.
The precipitate is black due to the formation of copper(II) sulfide (CuS).
The precipitate is not blue.

questions.explanation: When H2S gas is passed through an acidic solution containing Cu2+ ions, copper(II) sulfide (CuS) is precipitated. CuS is a black precipitate, characteristic of Group II cations like Cu2+, Pb2+, Hg2+, and Bi3+.
questions.subject: kvpy-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following reagents will produce a yellow precipitate when added to a solution containing lead(II) ions?

options.explanation: Potassium iodide does not produce a yellow precipitate with lead(II) ions.
Sodium hydroxide does not produce a yellow precipitate with lead(II) ions.
Ammonium hydroxide does not produce a yellow precipitate with lead(II) ions.
Potassium chromate produces a yellow precipitate of lead chromate (PbCrO₄) with lead(II) ions.

questions.explanation: Lead(II) ions form a yellow precipitate of lead chromate (PbCrO₄) when potassium chromate is added.
questions.subject: kvpy-chemistry

questions.question: In the qualitative analysis of a salt, a student observes that the salt is soluble in water and gives a white precipitate with dilute hydrochloric acid, which dissolves in excess ammonia. The salt is most likely:

options.explanation: Barium chloride does not match the description.
Lead(II) nitrate does not match the description.
Zinc sulphate does not match the description.
Aluminium chloride matches the description.

questions.explanation: Aluminium chloride forms a white precipitate of Al(OH)₃ with NH₄OH, which dissolves in excess ammonia due to the formation of the soluble complex [Al(NH₃)₄]²⁺.
questions.subject: kvpy-chemistry

questions.question: When hydrogen sulfide gas is passed through an acidic solution containing copper(II) ions, the color of the solution changes due to the formation of:

options.explanation: Cu(OH)₂ is not formed in acidic medium.
CuS is formed in acidic medium.
Cu₂O is not formed in acidic medium.
CuCO₃ is not formed in acidic medium.

questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ ions react with H₂S in acidic medium to form black copper(II) sulfide (CuS), which is insoluble.
questions.subject: kvpy-chemistry

questions.question: A student performs the flame test on a salt and observes a lilac-colored flame. The salt is most likely:

options.explanation: Sodium chloride produces a yellow flame.
Potassium chloride produces a lilac flame.
Calcium chloride produces an orange-red flame.
Strontium chloride produces a crimson flame.

questions.explanation: Lilac flame is characteristic of potassium ions (K⁺) due to the emission of 766.5 nm and 769.9 nm wavelengths.
questions.subject: kvpy-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct about the qualitative analysis of Group IV cations (Zn²⁺, Mn²⁺, Ni²⁺, Co²⁺)?

options.text: They are precipitated as sulfides in acidic medium
options.explanation: Group IV cations are not precipitated as sulfides in acidic medium.

options.text: They form insoluble hydroxides with NH₄OH in the presence of NH₄Cl
options.explanation: Group IV cations form insoluble hydroxides with NH₄OH in the presence of NH₄Cl.

options.text: They are precipitated as carbonates in neutral medium
options.explanation: Group IV cations are not precipitated as carbonates in neutral medium.

options.text: They do not form complexes with ammonia
options.explanation: Group IV cations can form complexes with ammonia.

questions.explanation: Group IV cations form insoluble hydroxides (e.g., Zn(OH)₂, Mn(OH)₂) when NH₄OH is added to their solutions in the presence of NH₄Cl to prevent precipitation of Group V cations.
questions.subject: kvpy-chemistry

questions.question: A colorless gas is evolved when a salt is treated with concentrated sulfuric acid and copper turnings. The gas turns moist blue litmus paper red and then bleaches it. The salt is most likely:

options.explanation: Sodium chloride does not produce bromine vapor.
Potassium bromide produces bromine vapor.
Ammonium nitrate does not produce bromine vapor.
Calcium carbonate does not produce bromine vapor.

questions.explanation: Potassium bromide reacts with concentrated H₂SO₄ and Cu to produce bromine vapor (Br₂), which is reddish-brown but appears as a reddish vapor that bleaches litmus paper due to its oxidizing nature.

questions.question: In the Lassaigne’s test for nitrogen, the Prussian blue color is due to the formation of:

options.explanation: Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃ is the correct compound.
Na₃[Fe(CN)₆] is not the correct compound.
Fe(CN)₂ is not the correct compound.
FeSO₄·(NH₄)₂SO₄·6H₂O is not the correct compound.

questions.explanation: The Prussian blue color is due to the formation of iron(III) hexacyanoferrate(II), Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃, when Fe²⁺ ions react with [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ ions in the presence of excess Fe³⁺.
questions.subject: kvpy-chemistry

questions.question: A student adds sodium hydroxide solution to a salt solution and observes a white gelatinous precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH. The cation is most likely:

options.explanation: Fe³⁺ does not form a white gelatinous precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH.
Cu²⁺ does not form a white gelatinous precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH.
Al³⁺ forms a white gelatinous precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH.
Ca²⁺ does not form a white gelatinous precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH.

questions.explanation: Al³⁺ forms a white gelatinous precipitate of Al(OH)₃ with NaOH, which dissolves in excess NaOH to form [Al(OH)₄]⁻.

questions.question: When a solution of sodium cobaltinitrite is added to a solution containing potassium ions, a yellow precipitate is formed. The formula of the precipitate is:

options.explanation: K₂[Co(NO₂)₆] is the correct formula.
K₃[Co(NO₂)₆] is not the correct formula.
NaK₂[Co(NO₂)₆] is not the correct formula.
Na₃[Co(NO₂)₆] is not the correct formula.

questions.explanation: The yellow precipitate is potassium sodium cobaltinitrite, K₂Na[Co(NO₂)₆], commonly written as K₂[Co(NO₂)₆] for simplicity.

questions.question: A student performs the borax bead test and observes a blue bead in the oxidizing flame. The metal ion present in the salt is most likely:

options.explanation: Cr³⁺ forms a blue bead in the oxidizing flame.
Co²⁺ does not form a blue bead in the oxidizing flame.
Fe³⁺ does not form a blue bead in the oxidizing flame.
Cu²⁺ does not form a blue bead in the oxidizing flame.

questions.explanation: In the borax bead test, chromium(III) ions form a blue bead in the oxidizing flame due to the formation of sodium metaborate and chromium metaborate.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of using ammonia in the qualitative analysis of metal ions?

options.explanation: Ammonia increases the pH of the solution, allowing metal ions to react with hydroxide ions and form insoluble hydroxides.

options.text: To reduce metal ions to their elemental form
options.explanation: Ammonia is not typically used as a reducing agent in qualitative analysis.

options.text: To oxidize metal ions to their highest oxidation state
options.explanation: Ammonia is not typically used as an oxidizing agent in qualitative analysis.

options.text: To complex with metal ions and prevent precipitation
options.explanation: While ammonia can complex with metal ions, its primary purpose in qualitative analysis is to precipitate metal hydroxides.

questions.explanation: Ammonia is used to precipitate metal hydroxides by increasing the pH of the solution, allowing the metal ions to react with hydroxide ions and form insoluble hydroxides.

questions.question: A salt gives a white precipitate with silver nitrate solution, which turns black on exposure to light. The cation in the salt is most likely:

options.explanation: The white precipitate that turns black on exposure to light is characteristic of silver chloride.
Silver bromide is also sensitive to light, but it does not typically produce a white precipitate that turns black.
Silver iodide is not typically associated with a white precipitate that turns black on exposure to light.
Silver sulfide is not typically associated with a white precipitate that turns black on exposure to light.

questions.explanation: The white precipitate that turns black on exposure to light indicates the presence of silver chloride, which is sensitive to light and decomposes to form silver metal.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is TRUE about the flame test?

options.text: The color of the flame is due to the emission spectrum of the metal ion
options.explanation: The emission spectrum of the metal ion is responsible for the color of the flame in the flame test.

options.text: The color of the flame is due to the absorption spectrum of the metal ion
options.explanation: The absorption spectrum is not directly related to the color of the flame in the flame test.

options.text: The flame test is only used to detect alkali metals
options.explanation: The flame test can be used to detect a variety of metal ions, not just alkali metals.

options.text: The flame test is only used to detect alkaline earth metals
options.explanation: The flame test can be used to detect a variety of metal ions, not just alkaline earth metals.

questions.explanation: The flame test works on the principle that when a metal ion is heated, it emits energy at specific wavelengths, which corresponds to the emission spectrum of the metal ion.

questions.question: A mixture of ions contains Cu2+, Fe3+, and Zn2+. Which reagent would be used to separate Cu2+ from the other two ions?

options.explanation: Cu2+ forms a black precipitate of CuS, while Fe3+ and Zn2+ do not react with H2S in acidic medium.
NH4OH in basic medium is not typically used to separate Cu2+ from Fe3+ and Zn2+.
KCN in basic medium is not typically used to separate Cu2+ from Fe3+ and Zn2+.
NaOH in basic medium is not typically used to separate Cu2+ from Fe3+ and Zn2+.

questions.explanation: Cu2+ can be separated from Fe3+ and Zn2+ by using H2S in an acidic medium.

options.explanation: Sodium carbonate is used to precipitate metal carbonates, such as Ca2+, Sr2+, and Ba2+.
While sodium carbonate can increase the pH of the solution, its primary purpose is to precipitate metal carbonates.

options.text: To reduce metal ions to their elemental form
options.explanation: Sodium carbonate is not typically used as a reducing agent in qualitative analysis.

options.text: To oxidize metal ions to their highest oxidation state
options.explanation: Sodium carbonate is not typically used as an oxidizing agent in qualitative analysis.

questions.explanation: Sodium carbonate is added to a solution containing metal ions to precipitate metal carbonates.

questions.question: A solution contains the ions Pb2+, Cu2+, and Fe3+. Which of the following reagents would be used to precipitate Pb2+?

options.explanation: H2S in acidic medium is not typically used to precipitate Pb2+.
H2S in basic medium is not typically used to precipitate Pb2+.
Pb2+ forms a yellow precipitate of PbCrO4 when treated with K2CrO4 in an acidic medium.
NH4Cl in basic medium is not typically used to precipitate Pb2+.

questions.explanation: Pb2+ can be precipitated using K2CrO4 in an acidic medium.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is FALSE about the use of dimethylglyoxime in qualitative analysis?

options.text: It is used to detect Ni2+
options.explanation: Dimethylglyoxime is indeed used to detect Ni2+.

options.text: It is used to detect Co2+
options.explanation: While dimethylglyoxime can react with Co2+, it is not typically used to detect Co2+ in qualitative analysis.

options.text: It is used to detect Cu2+
options.explanation: Dimethylglyoxime is not typically used to detect Cu2+ in qualitative analysis.

options.text: It is used to detect Fe3+
options.explanation: Dimethylglyoxime is not typically used to detect Fe3+ in qualitative analysis.

questions.explanation: Dimethylglyoxime is used to detect Ni2+, forming a red precipitate of Ni(DMG)2.

questions.question: A solution contains the ions Ag+, Hg2+, and Pb2+. Which of the following reagents would be used to separate Ag+ from the other two ions?

options.explanation: HCl in acidic medium is not typically used to separate Ag+ from Hg2+ and Pb2+.
NH4OH in basic medium is not typically used to separate Ag+ from Hg2+ and Pb2+ without first treating with H2S.
K2CrO4 in acidic medium is not typically used to separate Ag+ from Hg2+ and Pb2+.

options.text: H2S in basic medium, followed by treatment with NH4OH
options.explanation: Ag+ can be separated from Hg2+ and Pb2+ by using H2S in a basic medium, which precipitates Ag2S, HgS, and PbS, and then treating with NH4OH to dissolve the Ag2S.

questions.explanation: Ag+ can be separated from Hg2+ and Pb2+ by using H2S in a basic medium, followed by treatment with NH4OH.
